newsitem.title: USA: Two Pa. waste systems see diverging fates - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Two Pa. waste systems see diverging fates - S&P.

text.p: The divergent fates of two solid waste systems in Pennsylvania demonstrate what it takes to prosper following a Supreme Court decision that rocked such credits in 1994, Standard & Poor's Corp said Monday.

While the York County Solid Waste and Refuse Authority was able to maintain its single-A rating following the court's decision in Carbone vs. Clarkstown, S&P downgraded Lancaster County Solid Waste Management Authority's to BBB from single-A in 1994.
The court's ruling eliminated the ability of systems like the two in Pennsylvania to regulate flow control, which had previously been used to guarantee a steady stream of waste.
In the aftermath, rating agencies downgraded some systems that were especially dependent on flow control to maintain revenues backing bonds.
In the Pennsylvania analysis, published in Monday's edition of CreditWeek Municipal, S&P said York's rating survived the jolt because of several factors which distinguished it from Lancaster:
--York has a large percentage of its wasteflow under contracts where the municipality or contractor pays York directly for disposal. Lancaster does not.
--York held tip fees down and increased margins, whereas Lancaster has had consistently slim debt service coverage and charges above-market tip fees.
--Lancaster has consistently higher operating and debt service costs per ton due to the costs associated with building and operating its landfill.

"In the absence of legislated flow control, contractual wasteflow agreements insulate York from wasteflow losses," S&P said. "However, York faces the exposure of dependence on one contract wasteflow for 18 percent of revenues in 1995."
